# Milos Boat Tours: Which Type Should You Actually Book?

**Short answer:** choose the route before you choose the boat.

If Kleftiko is the main thing you want to see, a half-day or 6–7 hour west-coast trip may be enough. If you also want Polyaigos, expect a longer full-day experience. Choose a sailboat if the day at sea is part of the attraction, a speedboat if you want to cover ground quickly, and a catamaran if space and onboard comfort matter more.

The most expensive or longest itinerary is not automatically the best one.

The better question is:

**What kind of day do you actually want?**

## Choose the route before the boat

This is the mistake I would try hardest to avoid.

People often start with:

**Sailboat or catamaran?**

But that is not the first decision.

Start with:

**Kleftiko only?**

**Kleftiko plus Polyaigos?**

**Half a day or basically the whole day?**

Only then does the boat type really make sense.

A beautiful sailboat going somewhere you do not care about is still the wrong tour.

## If Kleftiko is your priority

Kleftiko is the obvious first boat destination on Milos.

White volcanic cliffs.

Sea arches.

Caves.

Clear water.

Swimming.

It is the place that appears in almost every serious Milos boat itinerary for a reason.

If this is your first boat day on the island and you mainly want to experience Kleftiko properly, I would not automatically pay for the longest route available.

Several tours spend substantial time there without turning the outing into a ten-hour expedition.

One current small-group sailing experience, for example, spends around **two hours at Kleftiko**, plus stops at Kalogries and Sykia.

That is already a serious day on the water.

## My slow-day pick: Oneiro sailing

The **Milos Oneiro Kleftiko sailing experience** is the kind of tour I would compare first if I wanted the boat ride itself to be part of the holiday.

It currently runs for about seven hours, leaves from Adamas and limits the group to 16 travellers.

The itinerary includes around two hours at Kleftiko, one hour at Kalogries and about 45 minutes at Sykia.

Breakfast, lunch and snacks are included.

Recent reviews repeatedly mention long swim stops, generous food and a relaxed pace rather than a rushed checklist of locations.

[Milos oneiro-kleftiko sailing experience with local guide](https://www.viator.com/tours/Milos/Milos-oneiro/d22323-345728P2?pid=P00320497&mcid=42383&medium=link&medium_version=selector "affiliate-button")

This is the format I would choose if I wanted to spend the day **on a boat**, not simply use one to reach Kleftiko.

## If you only want half a day

You do not necessarily need a speedboat to make a half-day Milos cruise worthwhile.

A current four-hour trip from Agia Kiriaki focuses on Kleftiko and Gerontas Bay, with views of several beaches along the south coast.

The main advantage is simple: you get the headline experience without giving the whole day to the boat.

That makes sense if:

* Kleftiko is your main priority
* you want time for something else later
* you are unsure whether you enjoy long boat days
* you prefer a simpler, shorter cruise rather than a long island-hopping itinerary

Four hours is enough to make the boat trip feel substantial without turning it into the only thing you do that day.

## My half-day pick: Kleftiko from Agia Kiriaki

The current **Half Day Boat Tour to Kleftiko Milos** lasts about four hours and leaves from Agia Kiriaki on the south coast.

It includes swim stops at Kleftiko and Gerontas Bay and passes beaches including Gerakas, Tsigrado and Firiplaka.

Snacks and local refreshments are included.

One practical advantage is the southern departure point: you are already much closer to Kleftiko than if you start from Adamas.

[Half Day Boat Tour to Kleftiko Milos](https://www.viator.com/tours/Milos/Boat-tour-to-Kleftiko-from-Milos/d22323-103214P12?pid=P00320497&mcid=42383&medium=link&medium_version=selector "affiliate-button")

I would choose this if I wanted **Kleftiko without giving up the rest of my day**.

## When Polyaigos changes the decision

Polyaigos is a different proposition.

It sits east of Milos and is famous for exceptionally clear blue water and remote coves.

Adding it usually means a much longer route.

That can be wonderful.

But it also means you are no longer booking “a Kleftiko trip with a little extra”.

You are booking a full sea day.

That distinction matters.

If you genuinely want both Kleftiko and Polyaigos, the longer itinerary makes sense.

If Kleftiko is the only place you really care about, the extra hours may not add enough value for you.

More stops do not automatically mean a better tour.

## Full-day catamaran: Kleftiko + Polyaigos

One current full-day catamaran runs for about **9 hours 30 minutes** and combines Kleftiko with Polyaigos.

Food, drinks, snorkeling equipment and guiding are included.

This is a very different product from the half-day speedboat.

It is not simply “better because it sees more”.

It suits someone who wants the boat to become the whole day.



[Catamaran Full Day Cruise: Poliegos - Kleftiko](https://www.viator.com/tours/Milos/Dreamy-Private-Cruises/d22323-31391P2?pid=P00320497&mcid=42383&medium=link&medium_version=selector "affiliate-button")

If I only had one boat day on Milos and loved being at sea, I would compare this seriously.

If I started getting restless after four or five hours on boats, I would not.

## Half-day vs full-day

This is a simpler decision than many booking pages make it look.

### Choose half-day if…

Kleftiko is the goal.

You want to swim but still keep half the day free.

You do not know whether you enjoy long boat trips.

You are already doing several full-day excursions.

Or you simply dislike the idea of being committed to a boat until late afternoon.

### Choose full-day if…

You enjoy being at sea even between stops.

You want Polyaigos or a broader island route.

A long lunch, drinks and relaxed swimming are part of the appeal.

You are happy for the boat trip to be the main event of the day.

Neither choice is more authentic.

They are just different holidays.

## Sailboat vs catamaran vs speedboat

### Sailboat

Choose this for the pace.

More time sitting, eating, talking and watching the coast move slowly past.

Some of the most memorable reviews are not about a particular cave at all.

They are about the crew, food and atmosphere onboard.

One warning:

booking a sailboat does not guarantee that the sails will be used continuously.

Wind, timing and route can require engine use.

Book the experience, not a fantasy of seven hours silently under sail.

### Catamaran

A catamaran often gives you more usable deck space and a comfortable setup for a long day.

That makes it attractive for full-day routes and groups.

But I would not write:

**catamaran = no seasickness**

because that is not something the evidence supports.

If motion sickness is one of your main concerns, I would read our separate guide:

**[Milos Boat Tours If You Get Seasick: Which Boat Should You Choose?](/milos-boat-tours-if-you-get-seasick-which-boat-should-you-choose/)**

The route, weather, duration and actual boat matter as much as the label.

### Speedboat

Choose it for efficiency.

It gets between stops quickly and can work especially well for a focused half-day.

It is also good if exploring caves and coastlines matters more than spending hours relaxing on deck.

The downside is the ride.

Chop that feels mildly noticeable on a larger boat can feel considerably more energetic on a fast smaller vessel.

## Departure point matters more than it looks

Most travellers naturally look at Adamas first.

It is convenient and many tours leave from there.

But some tours depart from the south coast or move guests there by minibus.

Why?

Because Kleftiko is on the southwest side of Milos.

Starting closer to it can reduce transit time.

That means two tours of similar duration can spend very different amounts of time at the places you actually came to see.

So I would check:

**Where does the boat really leave from?**

Not just:

**Where do I meet the company?**

Those can be different places.

## What “small group” actually means

This is another phrase I would ignore until I found the number.

Oneiro currently lists a maximum of 16.

The half-day speedboat has its own smaller-capacity format.

Other catamarans can carry more than twenty.

There is no universal definition of “small group”.

If avoiding crowds matters, look for:

**maximum passengers**

not adjectives.

That number is much harder to misunderstand.

## What is normally included?

Many good Milos cruises include some combination of:

* food
* wine or beer
* soft drinks and water
* snorkeling masks
* flotation equipment
* towels
* photos or drone footage
* transport to a changed departure point

But inclusions vary.

The Oneiro sailing trip currently includes breakfast, lunch and snacks.

The half-day speedboat includes refreshments and snorkeling equipment, and recent passengers mention complimentary photos and video.

Full-day catamarans usually include more substantial food and drinks because you are onboard for most of the day.

Do not compare two prices until you know what you are actually buying.

## Booking trap #1: the route can change

This is the most important condition on Milos.

Wind changes things.

Departure points can change.

Polyaigos can disappear from a route.

A north-coast section can be replaced by the protected south coast.

A good skipper adapts.

That is not a failed tour.

It is part of travelling by sea.

If one specific destination is the only reason you are booking, ask what happens if weather prevents it.

## Booking trap #2: “more places” can mean less time in each place

A ten-stop itinerary looks impressive on a sales page.

It can also mean:

arrive,

swim for twenty minutes,

leave.

That may suit you.

But if your dream is spending a long time at Kleftiko, I would rather know **actual stop duration** than total number of destinations.

Oneiro currently lists roughly two hours at Kleftiko.

That is much more meaningful information than a headline saying “discover the west coast”.

## Booking trap #3: the longest trip is not automatically the best value

Nine or ten hours sounds like more holiday for your money.

Sometimes it is.

Sometimes you are simply buying more transit.

A half-day speedboat can deliver an excellent Kleftiko experience because it covers distance quickly.

A seven-hour sail may provide fewer named stops but much more atmosphere.

A full-day catamaran earns its extra time if you genuinely want Polyaigos and a full sea day.

Value depends on what you wanted in the first place.

## Which type should you choose?

### First visit to Milos

I would make Kleftiko the priority.

A 6–7 hour sailing trip is probably my personal sweet spot.

Enough time to stop properly.

Enough boat to feel like an island day.

Still not a ten-hour commitment.

### Only half a day available

Speedboat.

Kleftiko-focused.

Simple.

### Couple who wants a relaxed day

Small-group sailboat or catamaran.

Passenger count would matter more to me than how many destinations appear in the title.

### Family

I would first ask how children cope with long days and swimming stops.

A six-hour catamaran may be much easier than nine and a half hours at sea.

If the children love boats and swimming, full-day becomes more realistic.

### Want Kleftiko and Polyaigos

Full-day.

This is the one case where I would stop trying to compress the itinerary.

The distance is part of the trip.

### Want maximum control

Private.

Not because private is automatically more luxurious.

Because you control the group and, within weather constraints, have far more influence over the rhythm of the day.

## Dan’s recommendation

I have not taken these particular Milos cruises myself.

I compared current itineraries, duration, passenger limits, recent reviews and weather conditions because the booking pages make it very easy to believe that a longer route with more stops must be the better choice.

I do not think that is true.

For a first visit, I would start with one question:

**Do I want to see Kleftiko, or do I want an entire day at sea?**

If the answer is Kleftiko, I would take the 7-hour Oneiro-style sailing day or the half-day speedboat depending on how much time I wanted to spend onboard.

If the answer is an entire sea day, then Kleftiko + Polyaigos on a full-day catamaran begins to make sense.

That is the rule I would use:

**Choose the day first.**

**Then choose the boat.**

## Before you book

Check:

* maximum passenger count
* actual departure point
* total duration
* estimated time at Kleftiko
* whether Polyaigos is included or weather-dependent
* food and drinks
* shade
* cancellation policy
* what happens if wind changes the route

And if motion sickness worries you, read the seasickness guide before paying.

A good Milos boat tour is expensive enough that spending ten extra minutes choosing the right format is worth it.

*Some links on this page are affiliate links. If you book through them, I may earn a commission at no extra cost to you.*

**Checked: 26 October 2026.**
